sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Server-Sent Events (SSE) is an HTTP-based unidirectional push protocol in which the client opens a single long-lived GET request to a `text/event-stream` endpoint and the server writes a stream of `data:`-prefixed events that the browser's native `EventSource` API receives, parses, and auto-reconnects with `Last-Event-ID` on disconnect.
Server-Sent Events were standardized in the HTML5 spec (W3C, 2009; WHATWG Living Standard) as a deliberately simple alternative to WebSockets for the common case where the server needs to push events to the browser but the browser does not need to push back. The mechanics are minimal: the client calls `new EventSource("/stream")`, the browser issues a GET to `/stream`, the server responds with `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and keeps the response open indefinitely, writing events as `data: <payload>

` chunks (each event terminated by a blank line). The browser parses each chunk, fires a `message` event on the `EventSource` object, and the application reads `event.data`. Events can be named (`event: update
data: ...

`) so the client can add specific listeners; they can carry an `id:` field that the browser stores as the last-received event ID and includes as `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect; they can carry a `retry:` field telling the browser how long to wait before reconnecting. There is no client-to-server channel — if the client needs to send data, it uses a normal fetch/POST to a separate endpoint. The protocol is so simple that the entire wire format fits in a one-page spec, and the browser API is roughly 30 lines of JavaScript to consume.

SSE matters because the majority of real-time web features are actually server-to-client only — live news feeds, stock tickers, status updates, notifications, log streaming, AI token streaming — and for these cases SSE is strictly simpler than WebSockets while having all the needed capability. **ChatGPT** uses SSE to stream each token as it's generated: when you submit a prompt, the server opens an SSE stream and writes one `data:` event per token (or per token-batch), so you see the answer forming word-by-word in real time rather than waiting for the entire response. This is the canonical use case for SSE in 2024 — LLM token streaming — and it's why SSE has had a renaissance. **Twitter** used SSE for its live tweet stream and live notification feed before migrating some of it to WebSockets for bidirectional features. **GitHub** uses SSE for its live Actions log feed (you watch CI logs stream in real time as your build runs) and for the live activity feed on dashboards. **LinkedIn, Slack's notification toasts, and YouTube's live comment stream** all use SSE for one-way push. The pattern is universal: any time the server has a stream of events and the client just needs to receive them, SSE is the simplest correct answer.

A real-world example worth studying is **ChatGPT's token streaming**. When the client sends a chat completion request, the server responds with `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and starts writing events: `data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Hello"}}]}

`, then `data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":" world"}}]}

`, and so on, one event per generated token (or per token-batch of a few tokens). The browser's `EventSource` (or a `fetch` with a streaming reader, since `EventSource` cannot POST) receives each event, parses the JSON, appends the delta to the displayed text, and the user sees the answer forming in real time. When the model finishes, the server sends `data: [DONE]

` and closes the stream. The benefits: perceived latency drops from "wait 10 seconds for the full answer" to "see the first word in 200 ms"; users can interrupt and redirect mid-generation; and the server can stream a multi-minute response without holding a single huge response body in memory. **GitHub Actions** does the same for CI logs: the build runs for minutes, logs stream over SSE as they're produced, and the user sees progress in real time rather than waiting for the build to finish.

The trade-offs and pitfalls deserve attention. First, **unidirectional only** — SSE cannot send data from client to server over the same connection; the client must use a separate POST. For purely server-to-client push this is fine, but for chat (where the client sends messages too) it's awkward — you end up maintaining both an SSE stream for incoming messages and a POST endpoint for outgoing, which is more complex than a single WebSocket. Second, **browser connection limit** — browsers historically limited 6 HTTP/1.1 connections per origin; opening 6 SSE streams would exhaust the limit and block all other requests on that origin. HTTP/2 multiplexing fixes this (all SSE streams share one TCP connection, so the 6-connection limit doesn't apply), but if your infrastructure doesn't support HTTP/2 end-to-end, this is a real problem. Third, **proxy buffering** — many reverse proxies (NGINX by default, some CDNs) buffer the response body until it reaches a certain size or the connection closes, which defeats SSE; you must disable buffering for SSE endpoints (`proxy_buffering off;` in NGINX, `X-Accel-Buffering: no` header). Fourth, **no binary support** — SSE is text-only (UTF-8); binary data must be base64-encoded, which inflates size by 33%. For text streams (logs, JSON, tokens) this is fine; for binary (images, video, binary protocols) use WebSockets. Fifth, **no per-message compression** — the connection can be gzip-compressed at the HTTP layer, but you cannot selectively compress individual events; WebSockets support per-message compression via the `permessage-deflate` extension. SSE connects to many other system design concepts: it is the modern replacement for long polling (Phase 2 Topic 14) for server-to-client push, it is simpler than WebSockets (Phase 2 Topic 13) when bidirectional isn't needed, it sits on top of HTTP (Phase 2 Topic 3) and TLS (Phase 2 Topic 5), and its `Last-Event-ID` resume pattern is essentially the same cursor-based replay pattern used in Kafka consumer offsets (Phase 6) and WhatsApp's message delivery (Phase 6 message queues).

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Browser (EventSource) participant S as SSE Server Note over C,S: One long-lived HTTP GET C->>S: GET /stream HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/event-stream S->>C: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
(connection stays open) Note over S: time passes, server has events S->>C: id: 1\ndata: {"msg":"hello"}\n\n S->>C: id: 2\nevent: alert\ndata: {"msg":"price drop"}\n\n Note over C: EventSource fires onmessage / onalert Note over C: connection drops at id=2 C->>S: GET /stream HTTP/1.1
Last-Event-ID: 2
(auto-reconnect) S->>C: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream S->>C: id: 3\ndata: {"msg":"resumed"}\n\n Note over C,S: Server replays events > 2, then live push resumes ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------+ GET /stream +-----------+ | Browser | Accept: text/event-stream | SSE | | EventSrc | --------------------------> | Server | +-----------+ +-----+-----+ ^ | | HTTP/1.1 200 OK | | Content-Type: text/event-stream | | (connection stays open) | | | | id: 1 | | data: {"msg":"hello"} | | | | id: 2 | | event: alert | | data: {"msg":"price drop"} | | | | (EventSource fires onmessage, | | onalert, readyState=OPEN) | | | | ... connection drops ... | | readyState=CONNECTING | | GET /stream | | Last-Event-ID: 2 (auto-reconnect) | |----------------------------------------->| | server replays events > 2, then live | | v Wire format (text/event-stream): +-------------------------------------------+ | id: 42 (optional) | | event: update (optional) | | retry: 5000 (optional) | | data: {"k":"v"} (required) | | | | (blank line terminates one event) | +-------------------------------------------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The browser creates `const es = new EventSource("/stream")`. The browser issues a GET to `/stream` with `Accept: text/event-stream` and opens a long-lived HTTP connection. The server responds with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`, `Connection: keep-alive`, and crucially does NOT close the response — it keeps the socket open and writes chunks as events arrive. The browser fires `es.onopen`, sets `es.readyState = OPEN`, and starts parsing the response stream. The server must flush each event immediately (disable response buffering in the framework — Node.js `res.flushHeaders()`, Python `yield` in a generator, NGINX `proxy_buffering off`); otherwise the event sits in a buffer and the browser doesn't see it. 2. The server writes events in the `text/event-stream` wire format: each event is one or more lines (`id:`, `event:`, `retry:`, `data:`), terminated by a blank line (`\n\n`). A simple event is `data: hello\n\n`; a named event is `event: alert\ndata: price drop\n\n`; a multi-line data event uses multiple `data:` lines that the browser joins with `\n`. The browser parses each event, fires `es.addEventListener("alert", ...)` for named events or `es.onmessage` for unnamed events, and if an `id:` was present, stores it internally as `es.lastEventId`. If the server includes `retry: 5000`, the browser will wait 5 seconds before reconnecting after a drop (default is 3 seconds). 3. When the connection drops (network glitch, server restart, proxy timeout), the browser automatically reconnects: it issues a fresh GET to `/stream` with the `Last-Event-ID: ` header. The server reads this header, queries its event store for events with id greater than the last-received, replays them in order, then resumes live push. This is the key reliability feature of SSE — the browser handles reconnection and cursor management natively, unlike WebSockets where the application must implement its own resume logic. If the server returns a non-200 status (e.g., 401 Unauthorized), the browser fires `es.onerror` and does NOT reconnect (the application must handle re-auth). To close the stream from the client, call `es.close()` — this sets `readyState = CLOSED` and stops reconnection.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers** - Holds recent events for replay on reconnect (Last-Event-ID). - Format one SSE event per the text/event-stream wire spec. - SSE demo const es = new EventSource('/stream'); es.addEventListener('message', e => log('message: ' + e.data)); es.addEventListener('alert', e =>… - Background thread that publishes events to the broker. - SSE (Server-Sent Events) server in pure stdlib. - Demonstrates: text/event-stream format, named events, - Last-Event-ID resume, retry directive, multi-line data, - And a simulated live event source. **Defines:** `SSEBroker`, `format_sse()`, `SSEHandler`, `ThreadingHTTPServer`, `simulated_publisher()`, `curl_demo()` ```python # SSE (Server-Sent Events) server in pure stdlib. # Demonstrates: text/event-stream format, named events, # Last-Event-ID resume, retry directive, multi-line data, # and a simulated live event source. import http.server import socketserver import threading import time import json import random PORT = 8765 class SSEBroker: """Holds recent events for replay on reconnect (Last-Event-ID).""" def __init__(self, retention=100): self.events = [] # list of (id, event_name, data_dict) self.next_id = 1 self.retention = retention self.lock = threading.Lock() self.listeners = [] # list of callable(event_dict) def publish(self, event_name: str, data: dict) -> int: with self.lock: eid = self.next_id self.next_id += 1 record = (eid, event_name, data) self.events.append(record) if len(self.events) > self.retention: self.events = self.events[-self.retention:] # Notify live listeners (parked SSE responses). for cb in list(self.listeners): try: cb(record) except Exception: pass return eid def events_since(self, last_id: int): with self.lock: return [(eid, name, data) for (eid, name, data) in self.events if eid > last_id] def add_listener(self, cb): with self.lock: self.listeners.append(cb) def remove_listener(self, cb): with self.lock: if cb in self.listeners: self.listeners.remove(cb) broker = SSEBroker() def format_sse(event_id: int, event_name: str, data: dict, retry_ms: int = None) -> bytes: """Format one SSE event per the text/event-stream wire spec.""" out = [] if retry_ms is not None: out.append(f"retry: {retry_ms}") out.append(f"id: {event_id}") if event_name and event_name != "message": out.append(f"event: {event_name}") # Multi-line data: each line gets its own "data:" prefix. payload = json.dumps(data) for line in payload.split("\n"): out.append(f"data: {line}") out.append("") # blank line terminates the event out.append("") # second \n => \n\n return "\n".join(out).encode("utf-8") class SSEHandler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_GET(self): if self.path.startswith("/stream"): self._handle_stream() elif self.path == "/": self._serve_index() else: self.send_error(404) def _serve_index(self): html = b"""SSE demo 

"""
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/html")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(html)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(html)

    def _handle_stream(self):
        # Parse Last-Event-ID from header (browser sets it on reconnect).
        last_id = int(self.headers.get("Last-Event-ID", "0"))
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
        self.send_header("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
        self.send_header("Connection", "keep-alive")
        self.send_header("X-Accel-Buffering", "no")  # NGINX: disable buffering
        self.end_headers()

        # 1) Send retry directive (tells browser to wait 3s on reconnect).
        try:
            self.wfile.write(b"retry: 3000\n\n")
            self.wfile.flush()
        except Exception:
            return

        # 2) Replay missed events if the client provided Last-Event-ID.
        for eid, name, data in broker.events_since(last_id):
            try:
                self.wfile.write(format_sse(eid, name, data))
                self.wfile.flush()
            except Exception:
                return

        # 3) Register as a live listener for new events.
        queue = []
        evt = threading.Event()
        def cb(record):
            queue.append(record)
            evt.set()
        broker.add_listener(cb)

        try:
            while True:
                evt.wait(timeout=15.0)
                evt.clear()
                while queue:
                    eid, name, data = queue.pop(0)
                    try:
                        self.wfile.write(format_sse(eid, name, data))
                        self.wfile.flush()
                    except Exception:
                        return  # client disconnected
                # Periodic comment-only heartbeat (keeps proxies alive).
                try:
                    self.wfile.write(b": ping\n\n")
                    self.wfile.flush()
                except Exception:
                    return
        finally:
            broker.remove_listener(cb)

    def log_message(self, format, *args):
        pass  # silence default logging

class ThreadingHTTPServer(socketserver.ThreadingMixIn,
                          http.server.HTTPServer):
    daemon_threads = True

def simulated_publisher():
    """Background thread that publishes events to the broker."""
    time.sleep(1.0)
    broker.publish("message", {"text": "Welcome to the SSE demo"})
    time.sleep(0.5)
    broker.publish("tick",    {"n": 1, "ts": time.time()})
    time.sleep(0.5)
    broker.publish("tick",    {"n": 2, "ts": time.time()})
    time.sleep(0.5)
    broker.publish("alert",   {"msg": "Price dropped 5%",
                                "symbol": "ACME"})
    time.sleep(0.5)
    broker.publish("tick",    {"n": 3, "ts": time.time()})
    time.sleep(0.5)
    broker.publish("message", {"text": "Multi-line payload",
                                "detail": "Line two of the data"})

def curl_demo():
    """Simulate a browser's EventSource with a raw socket."""
    import socket
    s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", PORT))
    s.sendall(b"GET /stream HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n"
              b"Accept: text/event-stream\r\n\r\n")
    s.settimeout(5.0)
    buf = b""
    deadline = time.time() + 4.0
    while time.time() < deadline:
        try:
            chunk = s.recv(4096)
            if not chunk:
                break
            buf += chunk
        except socket.timeout:
            break
    s.close()
    print("--- raw response from /stream ---")
    print(buf.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"=== SSE server demo (port {PORT}) ===\n")
    threading.Thread(target=simulated_publisher, daemon=True).start()
    server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", PORT), SSEHandler)
    threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    time.sleep(0.3)
    print(f"[server] listening on http://127.0.0.1:{PORT}/stream\n")
    curl_demo()
    # Demonstrate Last-Event-ID replay.
    import socket
    print("\n--- reconnect with Last-Event-ID: 2 (replays events > 2) ---")
    s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", PORT))
    s.sendall(b"GET /stream HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n"
              b"Last-Event-ID: 2\r\n\r\n")
    s.settimeout(2.0)
    try:
        buf = s.recv(8192)
        print(buf.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))
    except socket.timeout:
        pass
    s.close()
```

WebSockets are a full-duplex bidirectional protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection to a frame-based wire protocol.
